# Quantum symmetric pairs and universal K-matrices {#sec-qsp}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="Learning goals"}
- Know what a symmetric pair and a Satake diagram are, and which involution of $\hat g$ the boundary coideals of @sec-boundary-qg deform.
- Translate between the Letzter–Kolb coideals and the book's generators $b_j=e_j+q_j^{-1}f_jk_j+\hat\epsilon_jk_j$, including the parameter conditions.
- Understand why the special value $\hat\epsilon_j^2=\epsilon_*^2$ of @prp-an-k-existence is exactly the value at which a quantum Serre relation closes.
- Recognize the sine-Gordon boundary algebra as the q-Onsager algebra, and its Onsager limit.
- Know what universal K-matrices give for the reflection equation, and how generic irreducibility settles hypothesis (ii) of @thm-k-reflection.
:::

The coideal subalgebras of @sec-boundary-qg were found by physicists, who asked which non-local charges survive on the half-line. Mathematicians arrived at the same objects from a different direction. Noumi [@noumi1996], with Sugitani and Dijkhuizen in companion papers, and independently Letzter [@letzter1999], constructed quantum analogues of $U(\mathfrak k)$, where $\mathfrak k$ is the fixed-point subalgebra of an involution of $\mathfrak g$, as one-sided coideal subalgebras of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$. Kolb extended the theory to Kac–Moody algebras, including the affine ones that matter here [@kolb2014]. Since then the theory has acquired universal K-matrices [@balagovic_kolb2019; @appel_vlaar2022], a general construction of trigonometric reflection matrices [@appel_vlaar2025], and a (partly conjectural) classification of reflection matrices for the vector representations [@regelskis_vlaar2016].

This chapter places the physics coideals in that framework. Three results come out. The sine-Gordon boundary algebra, for every value of the boundary parameters, is a quantum symmetric pair coideal: the q-Onsager algebra. For $a_n^{(1)}$, $n\ge2$, and $d_n^{(1)}$ the diagonal case $\hat\epsilon=0$ is a quantum symmetric pair coideal, but the non-diagonal cases $\hat\epsilon_j=\pm\epsilon_*$ are not. They lie outside Kolb's parameter set, and they are the generalized q-Onsager algebras of Baseilhac and Belliard [@baseilhac_belliard2010]. The special value $\epsilon_*$ is precisely where an obstruction identified by Kolb vanishes, which gives an algebraic reason for @prp-an-k-existence. Finally, a theorem of Appel and Vlaar on generic irreducibility proves hypothesis (ii) of @thm-k-reflection for all the coideals of @sec-boundary-qg.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon=false title="What the rest of the book uses from this chapter"}
1. The boundary coideals of @sec-boundary-qg deform the fixed-point algebra of the Chevalley involution of $\hat g$, with Satake diagram $(\emptyset,{\rm id})$. For sine-Gordon every $(\hat\epsilon_0,\hat\epsilon_1)$ gives a quantum symmetric pair coideal, the q-Onsager algebra. For $a_n^{(1)}$ and $d_n^{(1)}$ only $\hat\epsilon=0$ does.
2. The special value $\hat\epsilon_j^2=\epsilon_*^2$ of @prp-an-k-existence is where a quantum Serre relation of the coideal closes (@prp-serre-obstruction). These coideals are generalized q-Onsager algebras, not quantum symmetric pairs in Kolb's sense.
3. Generic irreducibility proves hypothesis (ii) of @thm-k-reflection for every coideal of this part, when $q$ is not a root of unity (@prp-hypothesis-ii). It gives uniqueness of $K$, not existence.
4. Universal K-matrices exist for the quantum symmetric pair coideals and give the reflection equation directly; none is known for $\hat\epsilon_j=\pm\epsilon_*$.

@sec-trigonometric-k and @sec-generalized-satake are a guide to the mathematical literature. @sec-particle-reflection does not need them, except for its open problems.
:::

## Symmetric pairs and Satake diagrams {#sec-symmetric-pairs}

**Symmetric pairs.** Let $\theta$ be an involutive automorphism of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ and $\mathfrak k=\{x\in\mathfrak g\,|\,\theta(x)=x\}$ its fixed-point subalgebra. The pair $(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak k)$ is a *symmetric pair*. The simplest example is the Chevalley involution $\omega(e_i)=-f_i$, $\omega(f_i)=-e_i$, $\omega(h)=-h$. For $\mathfrak g=sl_N$ it is $X\mapsto-X^T$, and $\mathfrak k=so_N$. Every involution of a finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak g$ is, up to conjugation, described by a *Satake diagram* $(X,\tau)$: a set $X$ of black nodes of the Dynkin diagram, on whose subalgebra $\mathfrak g_X$ the involution acts trivially, and a diagram involution $\tau$, drawn as arrows. Kolb calls $(X,\tau)$ *admissible* if $\tau^2=1$, $\tau$ acts on $X$ as $-w_X$, and $\alpha_j(\rho_X^\vee)\in\mathbb Z$ for every white node $j$ fixed by $\tau$ [@kolb2014, Def. 2.3]. The involution is then

$$
\theta(X,\tau)={\rm Ad}(s(X,\tau))\circ\tau\circ\omega\circ{\rm Ad}(m_X),
$$

with $m_X$ a lift of the longest element $w_X$ of the Weyl group of $\mathfrak g_X$ and $s(X,\tau)$ a fixed torus element [@kolb2014, Thm. 2.5]. On the Cartan subalgebra it acts as $\Theta=-w_X\tau$. The algebra $\mathfrak k$ is generated by $e_i,f_i$ for $i\in X$, the $\theta$-fixed part of $\mathfrak h$, and $f_i+\theta(f_i)$ for $i\notin X$ [@kolb2014, Lemma 2.8].

**The affine case.** For a Kac–Moody algebra the relevant involutions are those *of the second kind*: $\theta(\mathfrak b^+)\cap\mathfrak b^+$ is finite dimensional. The Chevalley involution, which maps $\mathfrak b^+$ to $\mathfrak b^-$, is the basic example. Kolb shows that the admissible pairs classify the involutions of the second kind of any symmetrizable Kac–Moody algebra up to conjugation [@kolb2014, Thm. 2.7]. For $\hat g$ the involution $\theta$ of $g$ lifts to the loop algebra as $\hat\theta(x\otimes t^m)=\theta(x)\otimes t^{-m}$. The fixed-point algebras are the "twisted loop algebras of the second kind". For the Chevalley involution of $\hat{sl}_2$ the fixed-point algebra is Onsager's algebra, which appeared in his solution of the two-dimensional Ising model [@onsager1944] [@kolb2014, sec. 1]. For $\hat{sl}_N$ one obtains the $sl_N$-Onsager algebras of Uglov and Ivanov [@baseilhac_belliard2010, Rem. 1].

**Which involution do the physics coideals deform?** At $q=1$ the generators (-@eq-coideal-generators) become $b_j=e_j+f_j+\hat\epsilon_j$. In the vector representation of $a_n^{(1)}$ in the principal gradation, $e_j+f_j=yE_j+y^{-1}E_j^T$, and with $J={\rm diag}\big((-1)^i\big)$ the involution

$$
\theta(X)(y)=-J\,X(1/y)^T\,J^{-1}
$$ {#eq-chevalley-theta}

fixes every $e_j+f_j$ with $j\ge1$. It also fixes $e_0+f_0$ when $n$ is odd. When $n$ is even it does so after the additional loop rotation $y\to-y$ (checked in `textbook_code/qsp_checks.py`). So $\theta$ is the Chevalley involution of $\hat g$, conjugated by an element of the extended torus that changes the sign of every $e_j$. Its Satake diagram is $(X,\tau)=(\emptyset,{\rm id})$: all nodes white, no arrows. The diagonal coideal $B_0$ ($\hat\epsilon=0$) of @sec-coideal is therefore a quantization of $U(\mathfrak k)$ for this $\mathfrak k$. The constants $\hat\epsilon_j$ change nothing at $q=1$. As a unital algebra, $U(\mathfrak k)$ is generated by $e_j+f_j+\hat\epsilon_j$ just as well as by $e_j+f_j$ [@kolb2014, Cor. 2.9]. Whether nonzero $\hat\epsilon_j$ are allowed is a purely quantum question, answered in @sec-letzter-kolb.

The non-diagonal $a_n$ coideals behave differently. Since $(1-q)(1-q^{-1})=-(q^{1/2}-q^{-1/2})^2$, the special value of (-@eq-an-eps-condition) is $\epsilon_*=\pm i/(q^{1/2}-q^{-1/2})$, which diverges as $q\to1$. With $k_j=q^{h_j}$ one finds $b_j-\hat\epsilon_j\to e_j+f_j\pm i\,(\hat\epsilon_j/\epsilon_*)\,h_j$. In $sl_2$ the element $e+f+ih$ is nilpotent, while $e+f$ is semisimple, so this limit is not a fixed-point algebra of the Chevalley involution. We have not identified it. For the physics this is no defect: the physical $q=e^{-4\pi^2i/\beta^2}$ does not tend to 1 in the classical limit $\beta\to0$.

**Soliton-preserving boundaries.** A soliton-conjugating reflection matrix maps $V(\theta)$ to $\bar V(-\theta)$, and $\bar V$ is $V$ composed with the quantum Chevalley involution (@sec-an-diagonal-k). A soliton-preserving reflection matrix maps $V(\theta)$ to $V(-\theta)$. It needs an involution $\theta$ with $V^\theta\cong V$, so $\tau\ne{\rm id}$. Appel and Vlaar show that the standard (soliton-preserving) reflection equation arises when $\tau$ is the affine extension of the opposition involution, which fixes node 0, and the transposed (soliton-conjugating) one when $\tau={\rm id}$ [@appel_vlaar2025, sec. 7]. @fig-satake-involutions shows the two Satake diagrams for $a_5^{(1)}$.

![The two Satake diagrams $(\emptyset,\tau)$ of the physical reflection matrices of $a_5^{(1)}$, on the cyclic Dynkin diagram with the affine node $0$ drawn as a double ring. All nodes are white; none is a black node of a Satake diagram. For $\tau={\rm id}$ (the Chevalley involution) $\Theta=-1$ on weights and the multiplet $V_a$ goes to its conjugate $V_{h-a}$: soliton-conjugating. For $\tau$ the affine extension of the opposition involution, $j\mapsto-j$ modulo $6$, which fixes node $0$, $\Theta=-\tau$ reverses the coordinates $\varepsilon_i$ of the weights and $V_a$ goes to $V_a$: soliton-preserving. `textbook_code/figures/ch34_f29_satake_involutions.py` checks that the opposition permutation preserves the Cartan matrix of $a_5^{(1)}$, and its action on the weights of $\Lambda^a\mathbb C^6$.](figures/ch34_f29_satake_involutions.svg){#fig-satake-involutions fig-alt="Two hexagons whose six nodes represent the affine Dynkin diagram of a_5. ## Letzter–Kolb coideals {#sec-letzter-kolb}

**Kolb's generators.** Kolb uses the coproduct $\Delta(E_i)=E_i\otimes1+K_i\otimes E_i$, $\Delta(F_i)=F_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes F_i$ [@kolb2014, (3.3)–(3.4)], which is the coproduct of Part VI. For an admissible pair $(X,\tau)$ and parameters $c_i\in K(q)^\times$, $s_i\in K(q)$, the coideal $B_{c,s}$ is generated by $U_q(\mathfrak g_X)$, by the $\Theta$-invariant part of the Cartan subalgebra, and by

$$
B_i=F_i+c_i\,\theta_q(F_iK_i)K_i^{-1}+s_iK_i^{-1},\qquad i\notin X,
$$

where $\theta_q$ is a quantum analogue of $\theta$ [@kolb2014, (5.1)]. For $(X,\tau)=(\emptyset,{\rm id})$ this reads [@kolb2014, Ex. 7.6]

$$
B_i=F_i-c_iE_iK_i^{-1}+s_iK_i^{-1},\qquad \Delta(B_i)=B_i\otimes K_i^{-1}+1\otimes\big(F_i-c_iE_iK_i^{-1}\big).
$$ {#eq-kolb-generators}

This is a *right* coideal: $\Delta(B_{c,s})\subset B_{c,s}\otimes U_q(\hat g)$ [@kolb2014, Prop. 5.2]. The boundary of @sec-boundary-qg sits at the right end of the tensor product and needs a *left* coideal.

**From right to left.** The quantum Chevalley involution

$$
\omega_q(e_j)=f_j,\qquad\omega_q(f_j)=e_j,\qquad\omega_q(k_j)=k_j^{-1},\qquad \Delta\circ\omega_q=(\omega_q\otimes\omega_q)\circ\Delta^{\rm op}
$$ {#eq-omega-map}

is an algebra automorphism and a coalgebra anti-automorphism. It therefore maps right coideals to left coideals. It is also the map that defines the conjugate multiplet: $\bar V(y)=V(1/y)\circ\omega_q$ in the principal gradation (@sec-an-diagonal-k). (We write $\omega_q$ to distinguish it from the Lie algebra involution $\omega$ of @sec-symmetric-pairs, which carries signs.)

::: {#prp-omega-dictionary}
## Dictionary with Kolb's coideals
**[Proposition, sketch]** $\omega_q(B_i)=e_i-c_if_ik_i+s_ik_i$. Hence the book's coideal $B_{\hat\epsilon}$ of (-@eq-coideal-generators), with general coefficients $c_j$ of $f_jk_j$, is $\omega_q(B_{c,s})$ for

$$
c_j^{\rm Kolb}=-c_j^{\rm book},\qquad s_j=\hat\epsilon_j .
$$ {#eq-kolb-dictionary}

The parity-symmetric normalization $c_j^{\rm book}=q_j^{-1}$ is $c_j^{\rm Kolb}=-q_j^{-1}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Apply (-@eq-omega-map) to (-@eq-kolb-generators). That $\omega_q$ is an anti-coalgebra map is checked on the generators: $(\omega_q\otimes\omega_q)\Delta^{\rm op}(e)=1\otimes f+f\otimes k^{-1}=\Delta(f)$. All three statements, and the right-coideal property of (-@eq-kolb-generators), are checked on tensor products of $a_1$ and $a_2$ representations in `textbook_code/qsp_checks.py`.
:::

The antipode would also do: it maps $B_i$ to a multiple of $e_i-c_i^{-1}f_ik_i+c_i^{-1}s_ik_i$. That dictionary is $c^{\rm book}=-1/c^{\rm Kolb}$, $\hat\epsilon=s/c^{\rm Kolb}$, with the same invariant $\hat\epsilon^2/c^{\rm book}=-s^2/c^{\rm Kolb}$ (@exr-kolb-dictionary).

**Parameter conditions.** Not every $(c,s)$ gives a good quantum analogue of $U(\mathfrak k)$. Kolb requires that the only Cartan elements in $B_{c,s}$ are the $\Theta$-invariant ones, $B_{c,s}\cap U^0=U^0_\Theta$. This *intersection property* is what makes $B_{c,s}$ specialize to $U(\mathfrak k)$ [@kolb2014, sec. 10]. It leads to two parameter sets [@kolb2014, (5.9)–(5.11)]. The first constrains $c$ only when $\tau\ne{\rm id}$. The second reads

$$
\mathcal S=\big\{s\;\big|\;s_i\ne0\ \Rightarrow\ i\in I_{\rm ns}\ \text{and}\ a_{ij}\in-2\mathbb N_0\ \text{for all}\ j\in I_{\rm ns}\setminus\{i\}\big\},
$$

where $I_{\rm ns}$ is the set of white nodes fixed by $\tau$ and orthogonal to $X$. For $(\emptyset,{\rm id})$, $I_{\rm ns}$ is the whole diagram. Kolb calls $B_{c,s}$ with $c\in\mathcal C$, $s\in\mathcal S$ a *quantum symmetric pair coideal*. It is *standard* if $s=0$ and *nonstandard* otherwise [@kolb2014, Def. 5.6].

- **$a_1^{(1)}$.** Here $a_{01}=-2\in-2\mathbb N_0$, so $\mathcal S=K(q)^2$. Every sine-Gordon coideal $B_{\hat\epsilon}$, for every $(\hat\epsilon_0,\hat\epsilon_1)$, is a quantum symmetric pair coideal. It is nonstandard unless $\hat\epsilon=0$.
- **$a_n^{(1)}$, $n\ge2$, and $d_n^{(1)}$.** Every node has a neighbour with $a_{ij}=-1$, so $\mathcal S=\{0\}$. The diagonal coideals $B_0$ are standard quantum symmetric pair coideals. The coideals with $\hat\epsilon_j=\pm\epsilon_*$ are not quantum symmetric pair coideals in Kolb's sense.

As algebras they are nevertheless close to $B_0$. By Kolb's presentation of $B_0$ [@kolb2014, Thm. 7.1], $b_j\mapsto\beta_j$ defines a one-dimensional representation $\chi$ of $B_0$ exactly when $\beta\in\{0\}\cup\{\pm\epsilon_*\}^{r+1}$ (@prp-one-dim-modules). Since $B_0$ is a left coideal, $({\rm id}\otimes\chi)\circ\Delta$ is an algebra map $B_0\to U_q(\hat g)$ with $b_j\mapsto b_j+\beta_jk_j$, so $B_{\pm\epsilon_*}$ is the image of the standard coideal $B_0$ under this character twist. Dobson and Kolb obtain the nonstandard coideals from the standard ones in the same way for $s\in\mathcal S$ [@dobson_kolb2019, sec. 3.5], and it is @prp-boundary-module read backwards. Whether the map is injective we have not checked.

**The obstruction.** Kolb explains the condition $a_{ij}\in-2\mathbb N_0$ by a remark: if $s_j\ne0$ and $-a_{ij}$ is odd, the quantum Serre combination of $B_i,B_j$ acquires a Cartan term "in general", and then $B_{c,s}\cap U^0\ne U^0_\Theta$ [@kolb2014, Rem. 5.12]. For our case the term can be computed exactly. Write

$$
F_{ij}(x,y)=x^2y-[2]_q\,xyx+yx^2
$$

for the quantum Serre polynomial of two simply-laced adjacent nodes ($a_{ij}=-1$).

::: {#prp-serre-obstruction}
## The Serre relation of the boundary coideal
**[Theorem]** For a simply-laced $\hat g$, adjacent nodes $i,j$ and arbitrary $c_i,\hat\epsilon_i,\hat\epsilon_j$, the generators $b_j=e_j+c_jf_jk_j+\hat\epsilon_jk_j$ satisfy

$$
F_{ij}(b_i,b_j)=q\,c_i\,b_j+\hat\epsilon_j\Big((1-q)(1-q^{-1})\,\hat\epsilon_i^2-q\,c_i\Big)\,k_i^2k_j .
$$ {#eq-serre-obstruction}

For non-adjacent nodes, $b_ib_j=b_jb_i$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $b_i=e_i+\varphi_i+\hat\epsilon_ik_i$ with $\varphi_i=c_if_ik_i$. For $a_{ij}=-1$ we have $k_ie_j=q^{-1}e_jk_i$, $k_i\varphi_j=q\varphi_jk_i$, $\varphi_ie_j=q^{-1}e_j\varphi_i$, and $k_ie_i=q^2e_ik_i$, $k_i\varphi_i=q^{-2}\varphi_ik_i$, $\varphi_ie_i=q^2e_i\varphi_i-q^2D_i$ with $D_i=c_i(k_i^2-1)/(q-q^{-1})$. $F_{ij}(b_i,b_j)$ is linear in $b_j$; take its three terms in turn.

*The term $\hat\epsilon_jk_j$.* $F_{ij}(b_i,k_j)=\big(b_i^2-[2]\,b_i\sigma(b_i)+\sigma(b_i)^2\big)k_j$ with $\sigma(x)=k_jxk_j^{-1}$, so $\sigma(e_i)=q^{-1}e_i$, $\sigma(\varphi_i)=q\varphi_i$, $\sigma(k_i)=k_i$. A product $XY$ of two terms of $b_i$ comes with $1-[2]s_Y+s_Xs_Y$, where $\sigma(Y)=s_YY$. This vanishes for $e_ie_i$ and $\varphi_i\varphi_i$; for example the coefficient of $\hat\epsilon_je_i^2k_j$ is $1-[2]q^{-1}+q^{-2}=0$. The pairs $e_ik_i,k_ie_i$ and $\varphi_ik_i,k_i\varphi_i$ cancel after reordering. What remains is

$$
\hat\epsilon_j\Big[(1-q^2)\,e_i\varphi_i+(1-q^{-2})\,\varphi_ie_i+(2-[2])\,\hat\epsilon_i^2k_i^2\Big]k_j=\hat\epsilon_j\Big[-q\,c_i(k_i^2-1)+(1-q)(1-q^{-1})\,\hat\epsilon_i^2k_i^2\Big]k_j ,
$$

since $(1-q^2)e_i\varphi_i+(1-q^{-2})\varphi_ie_i=c_i(1-q^2)[e_i,f_i]k_i$.

*The term $e_j$.* In $F_{ij}(b_i,e_j)$ the part quadratic in $e_i$ is the quantum Serre relation. The parts quadratic in $\varphi_i$ or in $k_i$, and those linear in $\hat\epsilon_ik_i$, reorder to single monomials whose coefficients sum to zero ($q+q^{-1}-[2]$, $1-[2]q+q^2$, $2+q^2+q^{-2}-[2]^2$). The part linear in both $e_i$ and $\varphi_i$ leaves, after moving $\varphi_i$ to the right, $-q^2D_ie_j+e_jD_i=q\,c_ie_j$.

*The term $\varphi_j$.* In the same way only the part linear in both $e_i$ and $\varphi_i$ survives; the part quadratic in $\varphi_i$ vanishes because $F_{ij}(f_ik_i,f_jk_j)=F_{ij}(f_i,f_j)\,k_i^2k_j=0$. The surviving part gives $D_i\varphi_j-q^2\varphi_jD_i=q\,c_i\varphi_j$.

Adding the three terms gives (-@eq-serre-obstruction). At $s=0$ the weight-$\pm\alpha_j$ part is Kolb's (7.10), $F_{ij}(B_i,B_j)=-q\,c_iB_j$, transported by (-@eq-kolb-dictionary). In Kolb's conventions the result reads $F_{ij}(B_i,B_j)+q\,c_iB_j=q\,s_j\big(c_i-(q^{-1}-1)^2s_i^2\big)K_i^{-2}K_j^{-1}$. Both forms are checked on $V\otimes\bar V\otimes V$ of $a_2$, on $V\otimes\bar V$ of $a_3$ and on $V\otimes V$ of $d_4$, with random $c$ and $\hat\epsilon$, at the physical and a generic $q$ (`textbook_code/qsp_checks.py`).
:::

Three consequences follow.

1. **A boundary coideal that is too large.** If the bracket in (-@eq-serre-obstruction) is non-zero and $\hat\epsilon_j\ne0$, then $k_i^2k_j\in B_{\hat\epsilon}$. The coideal then contains Cartan elements that $\Theta=-1$ does not fix, and the intersection property fails. This is the algebraic form of the remark in @sec-k-intertwiner that at generic $\hat\epsilon$ the coideal is "too large" for an intertwiner to exist.
2. **The special value.** The obstruction vanishes for the pair $(i,j)$ if and only if $\hat\epsilon_j=0$ or $\hat\epsilon_i^2/c_i=q/\big((1-q)(1-q^{-1})\big)$. For $c_i=q^{-1}$ the second condition is $\hat\epsilon_i^2=\epsilon_*^2$. Suppose one $\hat\epsilon_j$ is non-zero. Then every neighbour $i$ has $\hat\epsilon_i^2=\epsilon_*^2\ne0$, so its neighbours do too, and on a connected Dynkin diagram the obstruction vanishes everywhere if and only if

$$
\hat\epsilon=0\qquad\text{or}\qquad\hat\epsilon_j^2=\epsilon_*^2\ \text{for all}\ j .
$$

This is exactly the existence condition (-@eq-an-eps-condition) for $a_n$, and the condition of @prp-dn-k for $d_n$. In Kolb's variables it is $c_i=(q^{-1}-1)^2s_i^2$. Regelskis and Vlaar call this the "q-Onsager type constraint" [@regelskis_vlaar2016, App. D].
3. **Generalized q-Onsager algebras.** At these values the generators satisfy $F_{ij}(b_i,b_j)=b_j$ for adjacent nodes and commute otherwise. Baseilhac and Belliard introduced the abstract algebras defined by such relations, the generalized q-Onsager algebras $O_q(\hat g)$. They found the same constraint as the condition for $A_i=e_iq^{h_i/2}+f_iq^{h_i/2}+w_iq^{h_i}$ to satisfy them, $\hat\epsilon_j=w_j=\pm i/(q^{1/2}-q^{-1/2})$ for $a_n^{(1)}$, $d_n^{(1)}$ and $e_{6,7,8}^{(1)}$ [@baseilhac_belliard2010, Prop. 2.1 and sec. 3.1]. With their symmetric coproduct, $e_jq^{h_j/2}$ and $f_jq^{h_j/2}$ are the book's $e_j$ and $q^{-1}f_jk_j$, so $A_j=b_j$ and $w_j=\hat\epsilon_j$. Their derivation came after the intertwiner analysis of Delius and MacKay [@delius_mackay2003, sec. 4.2], whose condition $|\hat\epsilon_i|=1$ is a slip for this one (@sec-boundary-qg-notes), and it was the first to state the value in the normalization $c_j=q_j^{-1}$. @prp-an-k-existence rederives it from the intertwining equation.

::: {#prp-admissibility}
## Admissibility and existence of K
**[Numerical]** For $a_2^{(1)}$, $a_3^{(1)}$ and $d_4^{(1)}$, and eight patterns of $\hat\epsilon$ (zero, all $+\epsilon_*$, one or two signs reversed, a zero mixed with $\pm\epsilon_*$, one value off $\pm\epsilon_*$, a single non-zero entry, random), the vector reflection matrix of @sec-soliton-reflection exists if and only if all obstructions in (-@eq-serre-obstruction) vanish.
:::

Checked in `textbook_code/qsp_checks.py`. The "only if" direction can be proved for the vector multiplets of $a_n^{(1)}$, $n\ge2$, and $d_n^{(1)}$, when $q$ is not a root of unity. Suppose the obstruction of the pair $(i,j)$ does not vanish, so that $\kappa=k_i^2k_j\in B$. Since $(2\alpha_i+\alpha_j,\alpha_i)=3$, the three elements $\kappa^rb_i\kappa^{-r}=q^{3r}e_i+q^{-3r}c_if_ik_i+\hat\epsilon_ik_i$, $r=0,1,2$, put $e_i$ and $f_ik_i$ separately into $B$. Hence $e_i(f_ik_i)-q^{-2}(f_ik_i)e_i=(k_i^2-1)/(q-q^{-1})$ and $k_i^2$ are in $B$. Conjugation by $k_i^2$ multiplies $e_m$, $f_mk_m$, $k_m$ of a neighbour $m$ by $q^{-2},q^2,1$, so $e_m,f_mk_m,k_m^2\in B$, and along the connected diagram this holds for every node. For $a_n$, $K:V(\theta)\to\bar V(-\theta)$ must intertwine every $k_m^2$, which acts on $\bar V$ as $k_m^{-2}$ does on $V$. So $K$ maps a vector of weight $\mu$ to one of weight $-\mu$, and for $n\ge2$ the vector representation has no such pair: $K=0$. For $d_n$, $K:V(\theta)\to V(-\theta)$ (@prp-dn-k) commutes with every $k_m^2$, so it is diagonal, $K={\rm diag}(d_\mu)$. In the principal gradation $K\,yE_m=y^{-1}E_m\,K$ then gives $d_{\mu+\alpha_m}=y^{-2}d_\mu$ along every non-zero entry of every $E_m$. The $E_m$ act irreducibly (@exr-generic-irreducibility), so some word in them of length $L\ge1$ has a non-zero diagonal entry, and $K=0$ unless $y^{2L}=1$. The converse is the existence part of @prp-an-k-existence and @prp-dn-k.

**One-dimensional modules.** A boundary bound state that is a singlet carries a one-dimensional representation $b_j\mapsto\beta_j$ of $B$, and its reflection matrix is the ground-state one with $\hat\epsilon\to\beta$ (@prp-boundary-module). Which $\beta$ are possible?

::: {#prp-one-dim-modules}
## One-dimensional modules
**[Proposition, sketch]** (i) Let $\hat g$ be simply laced with connected Dynkin diagram and at least one pair of adjacent nodes with $a_{ij}=-1$, and let $\hat\epsilon$ satisfy the condition of consequence 2, with $c_j=q^{-1}$. Then every one-dimensional $B_{\hat\epsilon}$-module has $\beta=0$ or $\beta_j^2=\epsilon_*^2$ for all $j$. (ii) For sine-Gordon every $(\beta_0,\beta_1)$ is allowed. (iii) **[Numerical]** In the $a_2$ and $a_3$ vector representations, $V(y)$ has no one-dimensional $B_0$-submodule for any $y$. For $s=\pm1$ it has exactly one, $\mathbb C_{\hat\epsilon}$ itself ($\beta=\hat\epsilon$), at $y^{n+1}=s(-q)^{(n+1)/2}$, with $(-q)^{1/2}=e^{-i\pi\omega/2}$ as in (-@eq-an-k-matrix). For $s=+1$ this includes $\theta=-i\pi/2$.
:::

::: {.proof}
(i) On a one-dimensional module, (-@eq-serre-obstruction) without the $k$-term becomes $(2-[2])\beta_i^2\beta_j=\beta_j$, that is $\beta_j\big((1-q)(1-q^{-1})\beta_i^2-1\big)=0$. Propagate along the diagram as in consequence 2. (ii) The q-Dolan–Grady relations (-@eq-q-dolan-grady) are identically satisfied by commuting numbers. (iii) Conjugate $V(y)$ by ${\rm diag}(y^i)$, so that the generators of nodes $1,\dots,n$ no longer depend on $y$. A one-dimensional submodule is a common eigenvector of these, and it lies in the joint kernel of their commutators. For each such vector, $b_0v=\beta_0v$ is linear in $(z,z^{-1},\beta_0)$ with $z=y^{n+1}$. Solved in `textbook_code/qsp_checks.py`.
:::

So in $a_n$ a singlet boundary state always belongs to one of the three classes $\hat\epsilon=0$, $s=+1$, $s=-1$, as the parameters of the ground state do. The submodule in (iii) is not the analogue of the sine-Gordon submodules at the bound-state poles (@sec-boundary-qg), which have $\beta\ne\hat\epsilon$. Here $\beta=\hat\epsilon$, and $\bar V(1/y_*)$ contains no copy of $\mathbb C_{\hat\epsilon}$, so the matrix (-@eq-an-k-matrix) has rank $n$ at $y_*$, with kernel $\mathbb C_{\hat\epsilon}$. Indeed, with $X=(-q)^{1/2}y$ and $N=n+1$, $\det K$ is a power of $X$ times $\big(X^N-s(-q)^N\big)\big(X^N-s\big)^{N-1}$ (checked for $N=3,4$ in `textbook_code/qsp_checks.py`). At the mirror points $X^N=s$ the matrix has rank one; for $s=+1$ and $\theta=i\pi/2$ ($X=1$) all its entries equal 1. This is the structure of a boundary-crossing pole, with the boundary coupling to a soliton–antisoliton pair, rather than of a boundary bound state. Whether the scalar factor has the pole has not been analysed.

**Torus-conjugated coideals.** The rescaling $e_j\to t_je_j$, $f_j\to f_j/t_j$ is a Hopf algebra automorphism. It maps $B_{c,\hat\epsilon}$ to $B_{c/t^2,\hat\epsilon/t}$, preserves the obstruction condition (it depends only on $\hat\epsilon_i^2/c_i$), and maps a reflection matrix $K$ to $\pi_{\bar V}(t)\,K\,\pi_V(t)^{-1}$ when $\prod_jt_j^{n_j}=1$. A general $t$ also shifts the spectral parameter, $y\to\lambda y$ with $\lambda^h=\prod_jt_j^{n_j}$. For example $t_0=-1$ maps the $s=+1$ coideal to the $s=-1$ one, and $K_{s=-1}(y)$ is a diagonal gauge transform of $K_{s=+1}(\lambda y)$ with $\lambda^{n+1}=-1$. Physically the two remain distinct, since a shift of rapidity is not a symmetry of the boundary. The rescaled parameters are Kolb's $c_j^{\rm Kolb}\ne-q_j^{-1}$, and Regelskis and Vlaar's "dressing" of a bare K-matrix [@regelskis_vlaar2016, sec. 7]. They are the source of the continuous free parameters of Gandenberger's $a_2$ and $a_n$ matrices ($g,h$, $d_i$, $E_i$) [@gandenberger1999a; @gandenberger1999b] and of Delius and George's families $K_\sigma$ [@delius_george2002]. In the physical, parity-symmetric normalization $c_j=q_j^{-1}$ they are absent (@sec-an-nondiagonal-k).

## The q-Onsager algebra {#sec-q-onsager}

For $a_1^{(1)}$ the quantum Serre polynomial has four terms, and the boundary algebra closes on itself, for every value of the parameters.

::: {#prp-q-dolan-grady}
## The sine-Gordon boundary algebra
**[Established]** [@kolb2014, Ex. 7.6] The generators $b_0,b_1$ of the sine-Gordon coideal, with arbitrary $c_0,c_1$ and $\hat\epsilon_0,\hat\epsilon_1$, satisfy

$$
b_i^3b_j-[3]_q\,b_i^2b_jb_i+[3]_q\,b_ib_jb_i^2-b_jb_i^3=\rho_i\,(b_ib_j-b_jb_i),\qquad \rho_i=q\,c_i\,(q+q^{-1})^2,
$$ {#eq-q-dolan-grady}

for $(i,j)=(0,1),(1,0)$. The left-hand side is $[b_i,[b_i,[b_i,b_j]_q]_{q^{-1}}]$ with $[x,y]_q=qxy-q^{-1}yx$. For $c_j=q^{-1}$, $\rho=(q+q^{-1})^2=4\cos^2\pi\lambda$ at the physical $q=-e^{-i\pi\lambda}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
This is Kolb's (7.19), transported by (-@eq-kolb-dictionary). Checked numerically in both conventions, on $V_{1/2}\otimes V_{1/2}$, $V_1$ and $V_{1/2}\otimes V_1$ with a boundary singlet, for generic $c$ and $\hat\epsilon$ (`textbook_code/qsp_checks.py`). Replacing $\rho$ by $1.1\rho$ fails.
:::

These are the *q-Dolan–Grady relations*. The algebra they define is the *q-Onsager algebra*. It appeared first in Terwilliger's work on tridiagonal pairs [@kolb2014, sec. 1]. Baseilhac and Koizumi named it [@baseilhac_koizumi2005a] and found it as the symmetry of the XXZ chain with the most general integrable boundary conditions [@baseilhac_koizumi2005]. Two features matter for the physics.

**The boundary parameters are not in the algebra.** The relations (-@eq-q-dolan-grady) do not contain $\hat\epsilon$. Every sine-Gordon boundary realizes the same abstract algebra, and the boundary parameters only fix its embedding into $U_q(\hat{sl}_2)$, through the counit value $b_j\mapsto\hat\epsilon_j$ on the boundary ground state. This is why the classical two-parameter family of boundary conditions survives quantization unconstrained. For $a_n$, $n\ge2$, the relation $F_{ij}(b_i,b_j)=b_j$ is also free of $\hat\epsilon$. But it holds only on the discrete set of consequence 2, so there the embedding is constrained.

**The Onsager limit.** At the physical $q=-e^{-i\pi\lambda}$, $q=1$ means odd $\lambda$, so the Onsager limit is not the classical limit $\lambda\to\infty$. At $q=1$, with $c_j=1$, (-@eq-q-dolan-grady) becomes $[b_i,[b_i,[b_i,b_j]]]=4[b_i,b_j]$. With $A=2b_0$ and $A^*=2b_1$ these are the Dolan–Grady relations

$$
[A,[A,[A,A^*]]]=16\,[A,A^*],\qquad [A^*,[A^*,[A^*,A]]]=16\,[A^*,A],
$$

which define Onsager's algebra [@dolan_grady1982; @onsager1944] (checked on loop-algebra representations in `textbook_code/qsp_checks.py`). The sine-Gordon boundary algebra is thus a deformation of the symmetry algebra of the Ising model. This explains its name. The values $q=1$ include the free-fermion point $\lambda=1$.

**Dynamical boundaries.** Baseilhac and Koizumi coupled boundary sine-Gordon to a quantum-mechanical system at the boundary [@baseilhac_koizumi2003]. The conserved charges keep the form $\hat Q_\pm=Q_\pm+\bar Q_\mp+\hat E_\pm q^{\mp T}$, but the $\hat E_\pm$ are now operators on the boundary Hilbert space. They derived algebraic conditions on $\hat E_\pm$ from the intertwining equation, their (19), and found a realization by Heisenberg operators. In coideal language the boundary is a tensor factor at the right end carrying a $B$-module $W$, as in @prp-boundary-module, with $\hat E_j=\pi_W(b_j)$. The coproduct (-@eq-coideal-coproduct) is then a coaction of $B$, and $W$ must represent the q-Onsager relations [@baseilhac_belliard2010, Prop. 2.2 and sec. 3.2]. Their (19), $[\hat E_+\hat E_-,\hat E_-\hat E_+]=c^2(q+q^{-1})^2(\hat E_+^2-\hat E_-^2)$, belongs to their ansatz (18) for $K$ and is stronger than the q-Onsager relations: $V(y)$ restricted to $B$ satisfies (-@eq-q-dolan-grady) but not (19). Their Heisenberg realization satisfies both, the q-Dolan–Grady relations with $\rho=c^2(q+q^{-1})^2$, which is (-@eq-q-dolan-grady) with $c_j=q^{-1}$ after their normalization $\hat Q=c\,b$, $\hat E=c\,\hat\epsilon$ (a numerical check, not included in `textbook_code`). Fixed boundaries are the one-dimensional modules, and by @prp-one-dim-modules (ii) every pair $(\hat\epsilon_0,\hat\epsilon_1)$ is one.

## The universal K-matrix {#sec-universal-k}

In the bulk, Jimbo's linear equations give the R-matrix on each pair of representations (@sec-sm-construction). The universal R-matrix explains why all these matrices solve the Yang–Baxter equation at once. For the boundary the analogous object is the universal K-matrix.

Balagović and Kolb define a universal K-matrix for a right coideal subalgebra $B$ of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ as an element $\mathcal K$ of a completion of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ that commutes with $B$ up to a twist $\varphi$ by a diagram automorphism and satisfies

$$
\Delta(\mathcal K)=(\mathcal K\otimes1)\cdot\hat R\cdot(\mathcal K\otimes1)\cdot\hat R ,
$$ {#eq-universal-k-coproduct}

where $\hat R=\mathcal R\circ{\rm flip}$ is the braiding [@balagovic_kolb2019, (1.1)]. This is the form for trivial $\varphi$. Otherwise the first $\hat R$ is replaced by its $\varphi$-twisted version $\hat R^\varphi$ [@balagovic_kolb2019, Def. 4.12]; their general construction gives $\varphi=\tau\tau_0$, which is not the identity for $(\emptyset,{\rm id})$ on $sl_N$. Because $\hat R$ commutes with $\Delta(\mathcal K)$, (-@eq-universal-k-coproduct) immediately gives the reflection equation $\hat R(\mathcal K\otimes1)\hat R(\mathcal K\otimes1)=(\mathcal K\otimes1)\hat R(\mathcal K\otimes1)\hat R$ on every pair of representations. No irreducibility is needed. With our left coideals the boundary factor is on the right, and the roles of the two tensor factors are exchanged.

::: {#prp-universal-k}
## Universal K-matrix
**[Established]** [@balagovic_kolb2019] Let $\mathfrak g$ be of finite type and $B_{c,s}$ a quantum symmetric pair coideal subalgebra, with parameters subject to the conditions that guarantee a bar involution on $B_{c,s}$. Then $B_{c,s}$ has a $\tau\tau_0$-universal K-matrix [@balagovic_kolb2019, Thm. 9.5], universal in the sense of (-@eq-universal-k-coproduct) when $\tau\tau_0={\rm id}$,

$$
\mathcal K=\mathfrak X\,\xi\,T_{w_X}^{-1}T_{w_0}^{-1},
$$

where $\mathfrak X$ is the quasi-K-matrix of Bao and Wang (an intertwiner between the bar involutions of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ and of $B_{c,s}$), $\xi$ acts on weight spaces by scalars, and $T_w$ are Lusztig's braid group operators.
:::

The formula needs the longest Weyl group element $w_0$, which does not exist in the affine case. Appel and Vlaar resolved this with the notion of a *cylindrical bialgebra*. Here $\mathcal K$ satisfies a reflection equation twisted by an algebra automorphism $\psi$ that need not respect the coproduct, $\Delta(\mathcal K)=J^{-1}(1\otimes\mathcal K)(\psi\otimes{\rm id})(\mathcal R)(\mathcal K\otimes1)$, with $J$ a Drinfeld twist. They construct such $\mathcal K$ for every quantum symmetric pair of Kac–Moody type, with an extra choice of a second generalized Satake diagram that selects $\psi$ [@appel_vlaar2022, Thms. 8.5–8.9]. In finite type they recover the Balagović–Kolb matrix. Their construction of the quasi-K-matrix avoids the bar involution and so needs fewer parameter conditions. The nonstandard parameters, however, are still restricted as in Kolb's $\mathcal S$: $\sigma_j=0$ unless $a_{ij}$ is even for all $i\in I_{\rm ns}$ [@appel_vlaar2022, sec. 6.8]. For quasi-split pairs Kolb and Yakimov gave an alternative construction, via star products, of a weakly universal K-matrix without the parameter constraints needed for the bar involution, for standard coideals [@kolb_yakimov2020, sec. 1.1] [@appel_vlaar2022, sec. 1.8.2].

For the physics coideals this means:

- **Sine-Gordon (all $\hat\epsilon$) and the diagonal coideals $B_0$ of $a_n$, $d_n$.** A universal K-matrix exists. Its image on the soliton multiplets is the reflection matrix, and the reflection equation holds by (-@eq-universal-k-coproduct), independently of @thm-k-reflection.
- **$a_n$ and $d_n$ with $\hat\epsilon_j=\pm\epsilon_*$.** These generalized q-Onsager coideals are outside all published constructions. No universal K-matrix is known for them. Regelskis and Vlaar list the study of their reflection matrices as future work [@regelskis_vlaar2016, Rem. 9.2].

The quasi-K-matrix generalizes the quasi-R-matrix: for the quantum symmetric pair of diagonal type, $U_q(\mathfrak g)$ embedded in $U_q(\mathfrak g)\otimes U_q(\mathfrak g)$ by the coproduct twisted with the Chevalley involution, it is Lusztig's quasi-R-matrix twisted by $\omega\otimes1$, in finite type [@bao_wang2018b]. Under the doubling trick a defect becomes a boundary of two copies of the theory, and its symmetry is a coideal of this kind (@sec-diagonal-qsp).

## Trigonometric K-matrices {#sec-trigonometric-k}

On a finite-dimensional representation of $U_q(\hat g)$ the universal K-matrix does not act directly. As for the universal R-matrix, one introduces a spectral parameter by the grading shift $\Sigma_z$ and obtains a formal series in $z$.

::: {#prp-trig-k}
## Trigonometric K-matrices
**[Established]** [@appel_vlaar2025, Thms. 4.2.1, 5.1.2 and 6.1.1] Let $U_q(\mathfrak k)\subset U_q(\hat g)$ be a quantum symmetric pair coideal, $\psi$ a suitable twisting operator, and $V$ an irreducible finite-dimensional $U_q(\hat g)$-module. Then:

(a) the universal K-matrix gives a $U_q(\mathfrak k)$-intertwiner $K_V(z):V(z)\to V^\psi(1/z)$, and the space of such intertwiners is one-dimensional;

(b) $K_V(z)=g_V(z)\,\mathcal K_V(z)$ with $g_V$ a scalar series and $\mathcal K_V(z)$ a polynomial (trigonometric) K-matrix;

(c) the $\mathcal K_V$ satisfy Cherednik's generalized reflection equation with the trigonometric R-matrices;

(d) every irreducible finite-dimensional module $V$ is generically irreducible under every *modified nilpotent subalgebra*, generated by elements $\tilde F_i$ with $\tilde F_i-F_i\in U^+U^0$, $i=0,\dots,r$. Here "generically" refers to the principal grading shift.
:::

For $\tau={\rm id}$ the reflection equation in (c) is the transposed one, for $\tau$ the affine opposition involution it is the standard one [@appel_vlaar2025, sec. 7]. For the q-Onsager algebra on the vector representation of $U_q(\hat{sl}_2)$, $\mathcal K(z)$ is the matrix of de Vega and González-Ruiz [@devega1993], our (-@eq-sg-k-coideal). Appel and Vlaar observe that its poles detect the reducibility of $V$ under $B$ only for generic parameters [@appel_vlaar2025, sec. 7.9].

Part (d) is what settles hypothesis (ii) of @thm-k-reflection. It needs no parameter condition. In book form, by (-@eq-omega-map), a modified nilpotent subalgebra is generated by elements $\tilde e_j$ with $\tilde e_j-e_j\in U^-U^0$. Every boundary coideal of @sec-boundary-qg is of this kind, whatever $c_j$ and $\hat\epsilon_j$: $b_j-e_j=c_jf_jk_j+\hat\epsilon_jk_j$.

::: {#prp-hypothesis-ii}
## Generic irreducibility of the boundary coideals
**[Proposition, sketch]** Let $q$ not be a root of unity, and let $c_j\ne0$ and $\hat\epsilon_j$ be arbitrary. For any two irreducible finite-dimensional $U_q(\hat g)$-modules $V_\mu,V_\nu$, for example soliton multiplets, $V_\mu(\theta_1)\otimes V_\nu(\theta_2)$ is irreducible under $B_{\hat\epsilon}$ for all $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ outside a proper analytic subset. In particular hypothesis (ii) of @thm-k-reflection holds, and an intertwiner $K_\mu(\theta)$, if it exists, is unique up to a factor for generic $\theta$.
:::

::: {.proof}
For generic $\theta_1-\theta_2$, $V_\mu(\theta_1)\otimes V_\nu(\theta_2)$ is an irreducible $U_q(\hat g)$-module. Shifting both rapidities by the same amount is the principal grading shift. By @prp-trig-k (d), transported by $\omega_q$, the module is irreducible under $B_{\hat\epsilon}$ over the field of functions of the shift. The proof by Appel and Vlaar is short. At the leading order of the shift, $b_j$ acts as $e_j$, and the $e_j$ alone act irreducibly [@appel_vlaar2025, Lemma 6.3.1 and Cor. 6.2.5]. By Burnside's theorem, irreducibility means that some words in the $\pi(b_j)$ span ${\rm End}$, which is the non-vanishing of a minor. The minor is a Laurent polynomial in $y_1,y_2$, not identically zero, so it is non-zero outside a proper analytic subset. Schur's lemma then gives ${\rm End}_B=\mathbb C$. The same argument for a single $V_\mu(\theta)$ gives uniqueness of $K$.
:::

This replaces the numerical checks quoted after @thm-k-reflection by a proof, for all the coideals of this part, including the generalized q-Onsager ones. The division of labour is now clear. Uniqueness and the reflection equation follow from generic irreducibility. Existence of $K$ is the real constraint. For quantum symmetric pairs, existence is guaranteed by the universal K-matrix. For the $a_n$ and $d_n$ coideals with $\hat\epsilon_j=\pm\epsilon_*$ it rests on the explicit solutions of @sec-an-nondiagonal-k and @sec-dn-vector-k.

## Generalized Satake diagrams {#sec-generalized-satake}

Regelskis and Vlaar relax Kolb's admissibility conditions [@regelskis_vlaar2016]. A *generalized Satake diagram* still consists of black nodes $X$ and a diagram involution $\tau$, but the associated automorphism $\theta$ need not be an involution. The subalgebra $\mathfrak k_c$ need not be a fixed-point subalgebra. What survives is the intersection property: the only Cartan elements in $\mathfrak k_c$ are those fixed by $\theta$. The corresponding *quantum pair algebras* $B_{c,s}$ are defined by Kolb's formulas, with Kolb's parameter sets. For $a_n^{(1)},b_n^{(1)},c_n^{(1)},d_n^{(1)}$ they classify the generalized Satake diagrams (families A.1–A.4, B.1–B.2, C.1–C.4, D.1–D.4 in their Table 4). They solve the intertwining equations on the vector representation in the homogeneous gradation, untwisted, $K(u)T_{\eta u}(b)=T_{\eta/u}(b)K(u)$, or twisted with the antipode and a transposition. Their Theorem 9.3 lists the bare K-matrices; all others are obtained by the torus dressing above. The theorem rests on computations for low rank and is a conjecture for general $n$ [@regelskis_vlaar2016, Rem. 9.2(i)]. They also conjecture that this classifies all solutions of the reflection equations with at most two non-zero entries in each row and column [@regelskis_vlaar2016, sec. 1.3]. Appel and Vlaar show that these matrices with $\tau(0)=0$, except for some $d_{2m}^{(1)}$ cases with $\tau\ne{\rm id}$, are images of universal K-matrices [@appel_vlaar2025, sec. 1.9].

The family A.1 is $(\emptyset,{\rm id})$. For $n\ge2$ its quantum pair algebra is standard, and the bare twisted K-matrix is the identity [@regelskis_vlaar2016, Thm. 9.3], the book's $K=1$ for $\hat\epsilon=0$. In their Appendix D they impose the q-Onsager type constraint instead of $s\in\mathcal S$ and obtain a dense matrix, which they attribute to Gandenberger [@regelskis_vlaar2016, (D.2)]. Their bare (D.2) is exactly (-@eq-an-k-matrix): after the gauge transformation ${\rm diag}(X^i)$ to the homogeneous gradation, it is their matrix with $u=sX^{n+1}$ and $q_{\rm RV}=q^{-1}$, for both signs $s$ (checked for $n=2,3,4$ in `textbook_code/qsp_checks.py`).

: Physical reflection matrices of this part and their quantum symmetric pair data. "QSP" means a quantum symmetric pair coideal in the sense of Kolb, with $c_j^{\rm Kolb}=-c_j^{\rm book}$ and $s_j=\hat\epsilon_j$ (-@eq-kolb-dictionary); "§" refers to the sections of `textbook_code/qsp_checks.py`. {#tbl-physics-qsp}

**The rational analogue.** For rational R-matrices (Yangians) the same story is simpler, and it came first in physics. For the principal chiral model on the half-line with boundary condition $g(0)\in H$, where $G/H$ is a symmetric space, Delius, MacKay and Short found the remnant of the Yangian symmetry [@dms2001]. It consists of the charges $Q^{(0)i}$ of $\mathfrak h$ and the twisted level-one charges $\tilde Q^{(1)p}=Q^{(1)p}+\frac14[C_2^{\mathfrak h},Q^{(0)p}]$, $p$ in the complement of $\mathfrak h$. These generate a twisted Yangian. The reflection matrix commutes with $\mathfrak h$, so $K_U(\theta)=\sum_W\tau_W(\theta)P_W$ over the $\mathfrak h$-components $W$ of $U$. The level-one charges relate neighbouring components $W_1,W_2$ by a branching-graph rule, the boundary analogue of the tensor-product graph [@dms2001, eq. (2.3)] (quoted, not checked here). MacKay and Short related the integrable boundary conditions of the principal chiral model, and their reflection matrices, to symmetric spaces [@mackay_short2003]. There the symmetric pair is visible classically, as the boundary condition itself. In affine Toda theory it appears classically as the automorphism $\sigma$ (transposition, the Chevalley involution up to sign) in the boundary condition of the Lax pair (@tbl-k-types).

## Exercises {#sec-qsp-exercises}

::: {#exr-omega-coalgebra}
Show that $\omega_q$ of (-@eq-omega-map) is an algebra automorphism of $U_q(\hat g)$ and that $\Delta\circ\omega_q=(\omega_q\otimes\omega_q)\circ\Delta^{\rm op}$ for the Part VI coproduct. Deduce that $\omega_q$ maps right coideal subalgebras to left ones. Show that $\bar V=V\circ\omega_q$ is the conjugate multiplet of @sec-an-diagonal-k.
:::

::: {#exr-kolb-dictionary}
Apply $\omega_q$ to Kolb's generator (-@eq-kolb-generators) and derive (-@eq-kolb-dictionary). Then use the antipode $S(e)=-k^{-1}e$, $S(f)=-fk$ instead, and show that $S(B_i)$ is proportional to $e_i-c_i^{-1}f_ik_i+c_i^{-1}s_ik_i$. Check that both dictionaries give the same gauge invariant $\hat\epsilon_i^2/c_i^{\rm book}=-s_i^2/c_i^{\rm Kolb}$.
:::

::: {#exr-serre-zero-weight}
Complete the weight-zero computation in the proof of @prp-serre-obstruction. Show that the coefficient of $\hat\epsilon_je_i\varphi_ik_j$ is $2-[2]q=1-q^2$ and that of $\hat\epsilon_j\varphi_ie_ik_j$ is $1-q^{-2}$. Explain why for $a_{ij}=-2$ (sine-Gordon) the weight-zero part of the Serre polynomial gives no obstruction. *Hint:* for $a_{ij}=-2$ the polynomial is antisymmetric under reversing the order of words, and its weight-zero part cancels in pairs [@kolb2014, proof of Lemma 5.11, step 4].
:::

::: {#exr-classical-limit-eps-star}
Show that $\epsilon_*=\pm i/(q^{1/2}-q^{-1/2})$ and that, with $k_j=q^{h_j}$, $b_j-\hat\epsilon_j\to e_j+f_j\pm i(\hat\epsilon_j/\epsilon_*)h_j$ as $q\to1$. Show that $e+f+ih$ is nilpotent in the two-dimensional representation of $sl_2$. Why does this not contradict the existence of a classical boundary condition with $C_j=\pm1$?
:::

::: {#exr-dolan-grady-limit}
In the spin-$\frac12$ evaluation representation of the loop algebra of $sl_2$, with $b_1=yE+y^{-1}F+\hat\epsilon_1$ and $b_0=yF+y^{-1}E+\hat\epsilon_0$, verify $[b_0,[b_0,[b_0,b_1]]]=4[b_0,b_1]$ directly. Show that the left-hand side of (-@eq-q-dolan-grady) is $[b_i,[b_i,[b_i,b_j]_q]_{q^{-1}}]$ with $[x,y]_q=qxy-q^{-1}yx$.
:::

::: {#exr-torus-dressing}
Show that $e_j\to t_je_j$, $f_j\to f_j/t_j$, $k_j\to k_j$ is a Hopf algebra automorphism, that it maps $B_{c,\hat\epsilon}$ to $B_{c/t^2,\hat\epsilon/t}$, and that it preserves the vanishing of the obstruction in (-@eq-serre-obstruction). How does a reflection matrix transform when $\prod_jt_j^{n_j}=1$, and what happens otherwise? Compare with @exr-torus-gauge.
:::

::: {#exr-one-dim-sg}
For sine-Gordon, show that every pair $(\beta_0,\beta_1)$ defines a one-dimensional representation of the q-Onsager algebra. For $a_2^{(1)}$ with $\hat\epsilon_j=\epsilon_*$, show that $(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2)=(\epsilon_*,\epsilon_*,0)$ does not, and identify the relation that fails.
:::

::: {#exr-generic-irreducibility}
Let $M(z)$ be the algebra of matrices generated by $z\,\pi(b_j)$, $j=0,\dots,r$, with $\pi(b_j)=z^{-1}A_j+B_j+zC_j$, so that $z\pi(b_j)$ is polynomial in $z$ with value $A_j$ at $z=0$. Show that if the $A_j$ act irreducibly, then $M(z)$ acts irreducibly for all but finitely many $z$. Apply this to the $a_n$ vector representation in the principal gradation, with $y=1/z$ and $A_j=E_j$: show that $E_0,\dots,E_n$ act irreducibly on $\mathbb C^{n+1}$.
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-qsp-notes}

Quantum symmetric pairs were introduced by Noumi, with Sugitani and Dijkhuizen in companion papers, for the classical Lie algebras, using explicit solutions of the reflection equation, with harmonic analysis on quantum symmetric spaces as the motivation [@noumi1996]. Letzter developed a uniform theory for all semisimple $\mathfrak g$ from the Drinfeld–Jimbo presentation [@letzter1999]. Kolb extended it to symmetrizable Kac–Moody algebras, gave the parameter sets $\mathcal C$, $\mathcal S$ and the defining relations, and noted that the q-Onsager algebra and the generalized q-Onsager algebras of Baseilhac–Belliard and Delius–MacKay are examples [@kolb2014, sec. 1] (as abstract algebras; the embeddings with $\hat\epsilon_j=\pm\epsilon_*$ are the character twists of @sec-letzter-kolb). The universal K-matrix is due to Balagović and Kolb in finite type [@balagovic_kolb2019] and to Appel and Vlaar for Kac–Moody algebras [@appel_vlaar2022]. Trigonometric K-matrices on all irreducible finite-dimensional representations, and generic irreducibility, are in [@appel_vlaar2025]. Generalized Satake diagrams and the vector reflection matrices of classical affine type are due to Regelskis and Vlaar [@regelskis_vlaar2016]. On the physics side, the q-Onsager algebra as a boundary symmetry is due to Baseilhac and Koizumi [@baseilhac_koizumi2003; @baseilhac_koizumi2005], and its higher-rank generalization to Baseilhac and Belliard [@baseilhac_belliard2010]. The rational analogue is due to Delius, MacKay and Short [@dms2001] and MacKay and Short [@mackay_short2003].

Remarks on the sources and on earlier statements in this part:

- **Kolb's Remark 5.12** says that for $s_j\ne0$ and odd $-a_{ij}$ the Cartan term is non-zero "in general". In book conventions it is the bracket in (-@eq-serre-obstruction), and it vanishes exactly at $\hat\epsilon_i^2/c_i=q/\big((1-q)(1-q^{-1})\big)$, the q-Onsager type constraint of Regelskis and Vlaar and of Baseilhac and Belliard.
- **Prior art for (-@eq-an-eps-condition).** Baseilhac and Belliard obtained $\hat\epsilon_j=\pm i/(q^{1/2}-q^{-1/2})$, equivalently $\hat\epsilon_j^2=\epsilon_*^2$, for $a_n^{(1)}$, $d_n^{(1)}$ and $e^{(1)}_{6,7,8}$ as the condition for the boundary charges to close on the generalized q-Onsager relations [@baseilhac_belliard2010, sec. 3.1]. This is the same as the existence condition of the reflection matrix (@prp-admissibility), and it also agrees with Delius and George's $d_n$ value (@sec-dn-vector-k).
- **Are the $s=\pm1$ coideals quantum symmetric pairs?** Not in Kolb's sense, because $s\notin\mathcal S$, but they are images of the standard coideal $B_0$ under the character twist $({\rm id}\otimes\chi)\circ\Delta$ (@sec-letzter-kolb), and they escape the obstruction that motivates $\mathcal S$. Regelskis and Vlaar state, without proof, that such coideals satisfy the intersection property [@regelskis_vlaar2016, Rem. 3.13(ii)]. Whether they admit a universal K-matrix, and what their $q\to1$ limit is, are open [@regelskis_vlaar2016, Rem. 9.2].
- **Hypothesis (ii) of @thm-k-reflection** is proved by @prp-hypothesis-ii, which uses only Appel and Vlaar's generic irreducibility theorem, valid for all parameters.
- **Conventions.** Kolb's coproduct is the Part VI coproduct. His coideals are right coideals and ours are left coideals, related by $\omega_q$ with $c^{\rm Kolb}=-c^{\rm book}$. Baseilhac and Belliard use a symmetric coproduct and generators $c_ie_iq^{h_i/2}+\bar c_if_iq^{h_i/2}+w_iq^{h_i}$, which equal $b_i$ for $c_i=\bar c_i=1$ and $w_i=\hat\epsilon_i$. Regelskis and Vlaar work in the homogeneous gradation with their own sign conventions for $c$ and $s$. Only $s_i^2/c_i$, the analogue of $\hat\epsilon_i^2/c_i$, is invariant.
